[NVIDIA] Compute distributed shared addresses unconditionally (#11794)

Compute distributed shared-memory addresses unconditionally with
`NVVM::MapaOp`, keeping the original predicates on the memory accesses.

ptxas implements `MapaOp` with a `PRMT` so predicating it creates an
extra `SEL` that just doesn't pay off. We instead emit it
unconditionally.

[AMD] Support GenericLinearLayout in FpToFpOp Conversion (#11791)

Previously when we do `tensor.to(dtype)` on a tensor with
`GenericLinearLayout`, the compiler tries to identify it as a canonical
LinearLayout and hit assertion.

It makes us add a specific LDS round-trip to convert layout before doing
FP conversion. Concretely, it happens in MoE/GEMM epilogue when we need
to convert the data type of accumulator who is in `GenericLinearLayout`.
This PR uses common getElemsPerThread function to avoid this issue.

[NVIDIA] Fix loading pointer elements from shared memory (#11771)

Implement loading a pointer from a shared memory buffer as loading an
i64 then convert to a pointer, consistent with the policy for shared
stores.

This makes pointer tensors work in general for all of
local_alloc/load/store/gather/scatter in both the IR and Gluon on the
NVIDIA backend.

Relax broadcast layouts (#11759)

There are multiple valid ways to broadcast a tensor with a given source
layout. Allow `BroadcastOp` to reflect that the destination layout can
be different from the source as long as no instructions have to be
generated to do the broadcast.

This is technically already expressible today by setting the source
layout to be the desired destination layout, but that is less convenient
and may not always be possible in `RemoveLayoutConversions`.

Fix operand layouts when absorbing view conversions (#11758)

In the case of reshape, `canUseResultEncoding` also requires that the
reshape's source encoding does not change. However, if the source
operand is also part of the backward slice, we could end up
rematerialising it with a new layout that might be incompatible with the
result encoding that we absorbed.

To fix this, record the desired encoding for the reshape's operand, so
that we skip rematerialisation if the value requires a conflicting
encoding.

[OptimizeThreadLocality] Handle multi-use thread locality results (#11682)

The thread-local reduction rewrite assumed the corresponding scf.for
result had one use. This will crash valid kernels that reused it in a
build with assert, and will lead to a miscompile without asserts:
```
lib/Dialect/TritonGPU/Transforms/OptimizeThreadLocality.cpp:342: virtual void
  mlir::triton::gpu::(anonymous namespace)::TritonGPUOptimizeThreadLocalityPass::runOnOperation(): 
  Assertion `loopResult.hasOneUse()' failed.
```

For example, we trigger this when `scf`.for produces `result` that is
used as both operands in and add operation like so:

```
    %result = scf.for ... iter_args(%acc = %zero)
    ..
    %twice = arith.addf %result, %result
```

This can very easily be triggered from source code with an almost
identical pattern.

The rewrite is checking that different values inside the loop have one
use, but it forget to check that loopResult.hasOneUse() and thus misses
that it can have multiple SSA uses, which all need to be replaced.

[LAYOUTS] Dispatch shared-layout lowering through `SharedEncodingTrait` (#11764)

### Problem

`TritonGPUDialect::toLinearLayout` lowers a shared layout by enumerating
the concrete encodings it knows about:
`dyn_cast<Swizzled/SharedLinear/NVMMA/AMDRotating/PartitionedShared>`,
otherwise `assert(0 && "unknown layout")`, where
`PaddedSharedEncodingAttr` already lands.

Yet every one of them already implements `SharedEncodingTrait`, whose
distributed counterpart has required `toLinearLayout` for a long time.
Adding a shared layout therefore means editing that switch instead of
implementing the interface.

### Change

Dispatch through that existing abstraction:

- shared-layout lowering asks the encoding through `SharedEncodingTrait`

This is the path `DistributedEncodingTrait` and
`SharedLinearEncodingAttr` already take - it just stops the call site
from naming concrete types.

[INTERPRETER] Honor round_f32_to_tf32 on host tensor descriptor loads (#11751)

A host `TensorDescriptor` created with `round_f32_to_tf32=True` makes
the TMA unit round every f32 it loads to tf32 (round to nearest even at
10 mantissa bits, Inf and NaN left alone), and
`RewriteTensorDescriptorToPointer` inlines the same arithmetic for
targets without TMA. The interpreter copies the flag in `_init_args_hst`
and then drops it: `_implicit_cvt` builds the `TensorDescHandle` without
it and `create_descriptor_load` returns the raw bits, so under
`TRITON_INTERPRET=1` such a kernel sees different values than on the
device.

This keeps the flag on the handle and rounds in `create_descriptor_load`
when it is set and the element type is f32. Gathers reuse that path.
In-kernel `tl.make_tensor_descriptor` never rounds, matching the pointer
rewrite.

The new test covers a tie that rounds to even, a tie that rounds up, a
mantissa that carries out into the exponent, and NaN/Inf. It passes on
an RTX PRO 6000 (sm_120) and under the interpreter with this change;
without it the interpreter run fails on 13 of 16 elements.

[Proton][AMD] Finalize the ROCprofiler client before process teardown (#11559)

This reduces flakiness for Proton's rocprofiler-sdk shutdown.

ROCprofiler-SDK can deliver buffered profiling records during process
shutdown. Proton previously allowed its profiler state to be destroyed
before that delivery was complete, so late callbacks could access freed
state.

The resulting failures were timing- and allocator-dependent: affected
processes could exit successfully, hang during teardown, report heap
corruption, or terminate with `SIGSEGV`/`SIGABRT` after profiling had
otherwise completed successfully. Explicit `proton.finalize()` often hid
the issue by draining pending records earlier, but process exit without
explicit finalization remained unsafe.

This change makes Proton’s lifetime agree with the ROCprofiler-SDK
client lifecycle: all callbacks required during terminal SDK shutdown
complete while their Proton destinations remain valid. It also adds
subprocess coverage for SDK-driven shutdown, using heap perturbation to
reliably expose stale- state access that would otherwise depend on
allocator reuse and timing.

The included regression test runs profiling in a subprocess, queues GPU
work, and deliberately exits without synchronizing the device or calling
`proton.finalize()`. This leaves rocprofiler-sdk responsible for
completing outstanding work and delivering pending callbacks during its
process-exit shutdown sequence, which is where the lifetime bug occurs.

The test also enables glibc’s `MALLOC_PERTURB_` debugging behavior.
Without it, freed Proton storage often retains enough of its previous
contents for the invalid callback to appear to work, making the bug
highly sensitive to allocator reuse and timing. I initially used a
simpler test that reproduced the original `SIGSEGV`, but only once
across many runs, so it was not reliable enough to demonstrate that the
fix changed the behavior rather than merely getting lucky.

With heap perturbation, freed allocations are overwritten with a
recognizable byte pattern, making callbacks into destroyed Proton state
consistently fail instead of accidentally succeeding. Running the test
for 10 subprocesses without the fix in this PR resulted in 10 failures
(non-termination during teardown, at least not within a generous
timeout). With the fix, 60 out of 60 runs exited successfully (well
under timeout).

[AMD] Avoid GIL deadlock during HIP library lookup (#11265)

## Summary

Loading of AOT cache is thread-unsafe on amd. 
Avoid a ROCm startup deadlock by replacing Triton’s dl_iterate_phdr
python
callback with a fully native callback compiled into the existing
triton._C.libtriton.amd extension.

This avoids entering Python while glibc holds its dynamic-loader lock
without
introducing a separately runtime-compiled helper.

Another approach would be to add native callback that is compiled in
runtime, but this seems a b it cleaner.

## Root cause

Parallel AOT-cache deserialization can create an ABBA deadlock between
Python's GIL and glibc's dynamic linker lock `_dl_load_write_lock`:

- Triton calls `dl_iterate_phdr()` through `ctypes.CDLL`, which releases
the
GIL for the native call. glibc acquires `_dl_load_write_lock` and
invokes
Triton's `ctypes.CFUNCTYPE` callback while still holding it. Entering
that
  Python callback requires reacquiring the GIL.

- Concurrently, another Python thread calls `hipModuleLoadData()`
through a
  native extension that has not released the GIL. HIP/HSA calls
`dl_iterate_phdr()` and blocks on `_dl_load_write_lock` while that
thread
  still owns the GIL.

This leaves one thread holding `_dl_load_write_lock` and waiting for the
GIL,
and the other holding the GIL and waiting for `_dl_load_write_lock` (as
shown in gdb and pyspy trace)

---------

Co-authored-by: Lei Zhang <antiagainst@gmail.com>
